title: Birds in a lotus pond

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of John M. Crawford Jr., 1988

altText: A long Chinese handscroll painted in black ink on satin. It shows birds in a pond with lotus plants, drawn with fluid, expressive brushstrokes.

context: A handscroll in ink on satin by Bada Shanren, also known as Zhu Da, made around 1690. He is remembered as one of the most original painters of early Qing China, known for birds, fish, and flowers drawn with very few, expressive brushstrokes.

descriptions.k: This long painting shows birds near a pond with lotus plants. It is made only with black ink. The brush strokes are loose and quick. Can you find a bird? What do you think it is looking at?
descriptions.g12: Bada Shanren painted this long scroll in China about 330 years ago. Birds sit near a pond with lotus plants. He used only black ink, but the strokes can look dark, soft, or wet. Where do you see thick lines and thin lines? How do the birds seem to feel?
descriptions.g35: Bada Shanren, also called Zhu Da, painted this handscroll around 1690 using only ink on satin. Birds and lotus plants share the scroll, drawn with bold, simple brush strokes. A handscroll is unrolled slowly, so you see only part at a time. Look at how thick and thin ink lines make birds and leaves. How can black ink alone create so much life?
descriptions.g68: Bada Shanren was a painter of early Qing China whose birds and plants are known for a bold, personal style. In this handscroll of about 1690, ink on satin creates shapes with a few confident strokes, and empty space matters as much as painted areas. Scholars often note that his birds have a distinctive, sometimes guarded look. How do ink tones, simple shapes, and space combine to give the birds character?
descriptions.g910: In Birds in a lotus pond, Bada Shanren uses spare, expressive ink on satin to turn a familiar subject into a distinctive personal statement. The handscroll's format encourages gradual viewing, while contrasts of wet and dry ink, bold and fine line, and filled and empty space create rhythm. His life story, as a former member of the fallen Ming royal family who became a monk and painter, has often shaped readings, but the painting should be weighed on its own visible evidence.
descriptions.g1112: Bada Shanren's handscroll of about 1690 exemplifies a calligraphic approach to painting, in which brush economy and ink tonality carry expression. Interpretations of his birds and plants have often drawn on his biography as a Ming descendant who lived through dynastic change, yet such readings are debated and can risk reducing the work to autobiography. The satin support and ink-only palette add material specificity. What can the visible brushwork, composition, and use of space support, and where does speculation begin?

teacherNote.context: A handscroll of about 1690 by Bada Shanren (Zhu Da), a leading individualist painter of early Qing China. It is painted in ink on satin.
directions: Have students paint a bird using only three or four brush strokes and compare how little is needed to suggest a character.
Discuss how an artist's biography can help or limit interpretation of an artwork.
Compare how the empty space is used here and in another East Asian artwork in the archive.
